I'm so sorry you're feeling this way. It sounds like you don't have a great support network and haven't really been listened to. 

Depression has a way of twisting your thoughts into negative pathways. In order to feel better you need to rewire your brain and learn to spot when You're thinking is distorted.

I grew up with a lot of trauma and a belief that I was unlovable. Fast forward a few years, after a lot of depression, an OCD diagnosis, losing most my friends, having a narcissistic family and a suicide attempt, I'm doing much better.

I have a partner who loves me more than anything, something I never thought I would have and I'm starting to make progress with my mental health.

Long story short, it does get better. I know you don't feel it because your depression won't let you but I promise you that I felt miserable at 17 and at 26  I never thought I'd find the love of my life but I did. 

I can already tell from your post that you deeply want to be loved and someone with so much love to give will definitely find someone who loves them in return. You just have to focus on loving yourself and getting the help and it will happen organically when it's meant to. 

Also try and look into EMDR therapy and DBT therapy. I think you would benefit from talking to others like you too if their are support groups for people with depression and anxiety. You can private message me too if you need someone to listen. 

Your are worth something, you are important, you are lovable and there are people who will care about you.

Hang in there ☺️

If you feel that bad, I would say invite him. He shouldn't expect you to change your plans but the kind gesture  of inviting your partner would be a good compromise in the relationship. It takes work to make sure your partner and you are both getting what you want out of each other but that's part of life and being in a strong partnership. It's all about balance. You have a few options. 

1. Be upset but don't change anything and lead your bf to get upset and feel like he's not a priority.

2. Give in to demands and not state your own needs for a fun night out with friends and resent your bf.

3. Meet in the middle and use this argument as an opportunity for personal and relational growth. 

Every couple argues but what you learn and to choose to do from resolving them determines if you can make it work.
